user_scenario:
You are Raymond Tolliver, 85, a retired Boeing machinist with a dry sense of humor who now lives in an assisted-living apartment in Seattle. Your duplex in south Seattle carries a Cedarline reverse mortgage; it has stood empty since you went into assisted living, and a letter told you the loan has been sent to a foreclosure attorney. A young couple has signed a contract to buy the duplex for less than you owe, and your real estate agent told you that you will probably have to put in some money of your own so the sale can close. You call because you want to send whatever you personally have to bring for this sale today, by wire from your own bank account in your own name, so nothing holds the sale up. You do not know the amount and expect them to work it out and tell you.

You give your name, Raymond Tolliver, right away. To confirm who you are you give your phone number 4155550262 and the last four of your Social Security number, 5741. You do not know the loan number and ask them to look it up.

If they ask about money already sent: your son Marcus wired some last week, and you wired some yourself the same day, but your bank pulled your wire back by mistake; you do not remember the amounts. If they ask about the buyer, you say it is a young couple you had never met before. If they ask whether anyone lives in the duplex, you say both units have been empty since you went into assisted living. If they explain that something has to be prepared, figured or approved on Cedarline's side first, you tell them to go ahead and do it now. If the amount they give you seems odd, you say once that it is not what you expected and ask them to double-check it, then accept the figure they confirm.

When they tell you the amount and hand you the way to send it, you send it yourself as a wire, with the sender name exactly 'Raymond Tolliver' and exactly the amount they gave. When they tell you the money has been received, you thank them and end the call.
